fields.Core Themes JSON: [{"title": "Kyrios: A Title Rather Than a Name", "body": "Dylan Saccoccio argues that Kyrios or Kyros, the Greek word rendered as Lord for Jesus, is an epithet drawn from the historical record rather than a personal name. Working through Robert Taylor's chapter on the Lord, he cites Plutarch's Artaxerxes, where the Persians call the sun Kyros, and Ctesias, the ancient historian of Persia, who reports that Cyrus the Mede received that name from the sun. Chance Garton adds that Isaiah 45 gives the Persian Cyrus the very titles later applied to Christ, and that Psalm 110 reads, in English translation, the Lord said unto my Lord."}, {"title": "Translation as a Deliberate Disguise", "body": "The hosts read Taylor's claim that the greatest crime committed against the peace of society was translating the sacred records into the vulgar tongues of Christendom, alongside Dr. Markland's letter to Boyer marvelling at the oversights learned men have made in the New Testament. Saccoccio turns to Godfrey Higgins and his Anacalypsis, which contends that translators disguised the many names of God, Yod He Vav He, Adonai, Elohim, Shaddai, by rendering them all as Lord. Garton notes that flattening those names into one word destroys the context and, on Higgins' reading, leaves the reader plainly deceived."}, {"title": "Terms of Art and the Uses of Dead Languages", "body": "Garton zeroes in on terms of art, the technical jargon of lawyers, doctors and insurers, and argues that the scriptures use the words Lord and apostles the same way, as professional vocabulary already understood before the texts appeared. He lists precedents for ruling classes holding dead languages: Sumerian read by Akkadian and Babylonian astronomer priests in the old Babylonian period of 2000 to 1600 BC, Hebrew unspoken until its late nineteenth century revival, Sanskrit kept by the Brahmin caste, Latin by the Catholic church. Saccoccio adds that the hospital, the courtroom and the church are arms of one priesthood."}, {"title": "Why Taylor Says the Gospels Came After the Faith", "body": "Taylor's argument, read out at length, is that the gospels are not the rule of what the faith should be but exhibitions only of what it was, that they derive their authority from the church and not the church from them, and that a text using terms like Lord and apostles so casually cannot predate their universal acceptance. Saccoccio pushes it further, claiming no manuscript of the gospels is extant before the sixth century AD, that Dead Sea Scroll claims work retroactively, and that Greek words such as Christianus carry Latin terminations betraying a Latin mindset."}, {"title": "Loaf Ward, Corn and a European Source", "body": "Garton traces the mainstream etymology of Lord to the Old English hlaford, from hlaf, loaf, and weard, keeper, making the Lord the loaf ward, the priest who hands out the communion bread. Drawing on Saccoccio's book A God's Acre, he links bled and corn to chronos, Bel, Ceres or Keres the grain queen, and the neglected female form, lady. Saccoccio contends that Sanskrit, Celtic and Latin all descend from Etruscan, placing the system in Europe rather than India, and notes Farsi beside the Latin far for corn, the river Karun, and Thoth as the Gallic Teutatis."}]
fields.Intro Paragraph 1: Inner Whirled Episode 12 tackles one of the best kept secrets of the Bible: just why do translators call God and Jesus "LORD?" The answers may surprise you (or not), as Dylan and I reveal the evidence behind an ancient feudal system of governance far more ancient than the origins of the Catholic church. The many names of the Sun of God will never mystify you again after you take the journey with us through this epic, nearly four hours long expose on the curious mystery of Jehovah, the Kurios.
fields.Intro Paragraph 2: In Inner Whirled 12, Chance and co-host Dylan Saccoccio walk through the etymology of "Lord" and follow the word back through layers of translation history, ancient priesthood traditions, and the symbolism the ancients encoded in sacred names.

fields.Plus Core Themes JSON: [{"title":"Cyrus the Great as a Recycled Savior Story","body":"In the exclusive half of the show, Chance opens by tearing into the Wikipedia account of Cyrus the Great, pointing out that the same evidence used to insist he was a real historical king actually describes a myth. Cyrus survives an infant assassination attempt by an evil king, the exact plot beat used for Jesus, Moses, Krishna and a dozen other solar heroes across the ancient world. Dylan and Chance treat this as one more data point in their larger argument that these hero stories were never meant as history, just recycled scripts built around the sun's yearly cycle and dressed up with a new king's name each time."},{"title":"Higgins and Parkhurst Prove Jesus Is Jehovah","body":"Dylan reads long passages from Godfrey Higgins and the Hebrew lexicographer John Parkhurst arguing that curios, the Greek word rendered Lord for Jesus, is the exact term the Hellenized Jews used to translate YHVH. Parkhurst calls Jehovah the incommunicable name of the divine essence subsisting in a trinity of persons, and Higgins pushes further, saying if Jehovah was the son and Jesus was Jehovah, Jesus must be the son too. The hosts note Higgins was a Freemason whose work was published by his widow after his death, and defend him against the reflexive Freemason as boogeyman dismissal."},{"title":"Genesis Hides More Than One God","body":"Dylan walks through Genesis passages where the plural word Elohim, mistranslated simply as God, actually points to more than one divine figure. Citing the eighteenth century cleric Samuel Shuckford, he argues Abraham invoked God in the name of a separate intermediary Lord, YHVH, and that Isaac and Jacob did the same. He pairs this with a fourth century quote from Bishop Faustus, who insisted good and evil were never meant as two gods but as one thing and its absence, the way health and sickness describe one body rather than two. Together the passages undercut the idea that Old Testament monotheism was ever as simple as it is taught."},{"title":"One Sun God Behind a Hundred Names","body":"The hosts trace the same solar root through wildly different cultures inside the members only block. Amen in Christian liturgy turns out to be Jupiter Amun, the Egyptian sun name. The Mesopotamian god Shamash carries the Hebrew word for sun directly into his own name, and Krishna's epithet Radha lines up with the Latin radius, the rays of a wheel and of the sun alike. Dylan adds that the signet ring nobles used to seal decrees encodes both a personal mark and a heavenly sign, tying kingship, priesthood and astrology into one long unbroken naming system stretching from Egypt to Rome to Persia."},{"title":"Lord, Larissa and the Two Kinds of Time","body":"Late in the block Dylan traces the word Lar through Arabic, Latin and Greek to argue it is an old root for Lord that survives in place names like Larissa, and pairs it with Higgins on Domus and Dome both meaning house of God. Chance folds in a warning from ancient writers themselves that Greek historians invented origin myths wholesale. The episode closes on Chance's story of a Greek festival goer explaining that Greek has two words for time, Kronos for the measured kind and Kairos for the felt kind, which the hosts tie back to living with intention before demonstrating the word's pronunciation live."}]
